about: Oldest schools, universities and colleges, hospitals, post offices, courts, police and fire stations, town halls and other public institutions of the isles (research track, 2026-10-22); each with the age claim, whether it concerns the institution or the surviving building, how secure it is, and sources with exact quotes (checked by python -m bidb.evidence --check).

entries.name: The King's School, Canterbury
entries.age_text: traditionally founded with St Augustine's mission in 597; teaching at Canterbury attested from the 7th century, refounded by Henry VIII in 1541
entries.claim: the oldest continuously operating school in the world
entries.evidence: The 597 date rests on tradition linking the school to St Augustine; its own Wikipedia article says the founding date is difficult to verify, and Bede only implies a Kentish school by c.630. Continuity through the Middle Ages is assumed rather than documented, and the present school dates from the 1541 refoundation; the claim is about the institution, not any surviving building.

With Ruthin School's closure in 2026 it is the oldest surviving school in Wales by foundation date.

entries.name: University of Oxford
entries.age_text: evidence of teaching from 1096; grew rapidly from 1167; chancellor recorded 1201, royal charter 1248
entries.claim: the oldest university in the English-speaking world
entries.evidence: There is no foundation date: 1096 is the earliest evidence of teaching, and the university as a corporate body is documented from c.1200 (first chancellor 1201, charter 1248). The claim is about the institution; its oldest purpose-built university building is the Divinity School (1427–83), though college buildings are older.

entries.evidence: 979 is a traditional date (the millennium was celebrated in 1979); documentary evidence begins in the 13th century, and Tynwald's own site dates the hill itself to Norse settlers of the 13th century. Iceland's Althing (930) is older but was suspended 1800–1845, hence Tynwald's claim to be the oldest continuous one; Tynwald itself words it as a claim.

entries.name: Palace of Westminster
entries.age_text: Westminster Hall 1097–99; Parliament met in the palace from the 13th century; present palace 1840–70
entries.claim: the home of the 'mother of parliaments'; Westminster Hall its oldest part
entries.evidence: Parliament has met in the palace since the 13th century, but the present building is Barry and Pugin's of 1840–70; only Westminster Hall (1097–99, roof 1393–1401), the crypt chapel and the Jewel Tower survive from the medieval palace. Tynwald is older as an assembly.

entries.category: Oldest town hall or seat of government
entries.name: Exeter Guildhall
entries.age_text: hall on the site probably from the later 12th century (deed of c.1160); present hall 1468–70, portico 1592–94
entries.claim: the oldest municipal building in England still in use
entries.evidence: The site has been Exeter's civic centre since at least the 14th century and probably the 12th, but the present hall was built in 1468–70, so the claim is to the oldest civic site in continuous use rather than the oldest building; London's Guildhall (1411) has an older surviving hall.

entries.name: Castle Rushen

entries.claim: the seat of government of the Isle of Man for some seven centuries
entries.evidence: The castle was the administrative and judicial centre of Mann until the capital moved to Douglas (1869–74); its oldest fabric is late 12th or early 13th century (a beam dated 947 is unproven). The Old House of Keys stands opposite.

entries.age_text: present Great Hall 1411–c.1440; a guildhall on the site recorded from 1128; crypts earlier
entries.claim: the City's only surviving secular medieval building, its town hall for nearly 900 years
entries.evidence: The present hall dates from 1411–40 (restored after 1666 and 1940); documentary references to a London guildhall go back to 1128, and the Roman amphitheatre lies beneath. It is still the City of London Corporation's ceremonial and administrative centre.

entries.evidence: The 1404 parliament at Machynlleth is historical, but tree-ring dating shows the present building is two generations later, and it was heavily rebuilt in 1906–12; the link to 1404 is tradition only.

entries.claim: Kilkenny's medieval-origin town hall, still the city hall
entries.evidence: Usually dated 1761, but the NIAH record shows a tholsel built 1695–98 that was rebuilt in 1759–61; the medieval predecessor (scene of Petronilla de Meath's execution in 1324) is tradition. No source claims it as the oldest town hall in Ireland.

entries.name: Parliament House, Dublin
entries.age_text: designed by Edward Lovett Pearce, begun 1729, first sitting 1731, completed 1739; Bank of Ireland since 1803
entries.claim: the world's first purpose-built two-chamber parliament house
entries.evidence: Pearce's building (1729–39) was purpose-built for the Irish Lords and Commons; Edinburgh's Parliament Hall (1639) was purpose-built earlier but for a single-chamber parliament, hence the 'bicameral' qualifier. It has not housed a parliament since 1800.

entries.claim: England's oldest charitable almshouse in continuous use
entries.evidence: The foundation is dated c.1132–36 and the Brothers have lived there ever since. St Oswald's Hospital, Worcester (traditionally c.990) and St Nicholas, Harbledown (c.1084) are older foundations, so 'oldest in continuous use as an almshouse in its medieval buildings' is the defensible form.
